newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Arabia says economic reforms are paying off.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Arabia says economic reforms are paying off.

text.p: Saudi Arabia told the world's top financial institutions that its economic reforms in the past few years were beginning to bear fruit and it expected 6.2 percent GDP growth this year.

Finance and National Economy Minister Ibrahim Abdel Aziz al-Asaf told the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank in Washington that Saudi Arabia was determined to press ahead with reforms, the official Saudi Press Agency reported late on Sunday.
It quoted Asaf as saying the "Saudi economy is beginning to bear the fruit of the wise policies that the government adopted in the past few years.
"Initial indications show that the growth in gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to reach 6.2 percent in 1996 compared to 4.2 percent in 1995," he said.

"There is also a big improvement in the balance of payment's current account due to an increase in exports including non-oil exports which went up by 10 percent in the first half of 1996 compared to the first half of 1995."
SPA did not say if he elaborated on the current account, but economists forecast a current account deficit of $2 billion to $2.5 billion for 1996, about half that of 1995, or even a small surplus.
Asaf said the private sector was beginning to play a bigger role amid a growth in industrial investment.

Saudi Arabia has in the past few years suffered cash flow problems due to low oil prices and Gulf War costs that prompted it to introduce reforms and tighten public spending. It is also trying to encourage a larger private sector role, privatise some government institutions and boost non-oil exports.

Economists and bankers say the kingdom expects to sharply reduce or even wipe out its budget deficit in 1996 for the first time in more than 10 years, as oil prices hover around their highest level since the 1991 Gulf War.
